title: Guardrails and Failure Containment

sections.title: Separating Interactive Requests From Batch Work
Circuit Breakers When the Cluster Slows Down
Rate Limits and the Caller Who Uses Them
State-Changing Operations Need a Different Refusal Contract
Applying the Controls to a Third-Party API
Design Exercise: Admission Control for a Reporting API

html:
A customer searching for a product expects results within a moment or two. A merchant downloading ten thousand product listings can usually wait for a file to be prepared. At Baodium, both operations were running through the same search application, and that difference in expectations had not been reflected in how the service allocated its resources.

The problem surfaced on the search dashboard a few weeks after the team introduced the observability improvements from Chapter 8. Search latency was increasing, although the search application had not been deployed that day. The engineers checked the cluster’s query rate and discovered an increase in requests from Catalog Export, a feature another team had added for merchants who wanted to download their listings as spreadsheets.

An export retrieved many pages of search results and assembled them into a file. During the worst intervals, six exports were running at once. Each occupied a worker for several seconds, while as many as forty customer searches waited in the same worker queue. Query execution inside the search cluster had also increased from roughly 60 to 150 milliseconds. Exports were occupying the application’s workers and generating enough additional queries to slow the shared cluster.

The engineers had two problems to solve. They needed to protect the workers that served interactive searches, and they needed to limit how much work exports could send to the cluster. Increasing the worker count would have allowed more exports to run while the cluster was already slowing down. Shorter timeouts might have ended individual requests sooner, but they would not prevent the next export from making the same demands.

This is the noisy neighbor problem: one workload consumes resources needed by another. We have encountered resource contention throughout the book, from database connections in Chapter 1 to fraud-provider capacity in Chapter 4. Here we will use the search incident to build the controls that keep different workloads within their allocations, including what happens when the dependency itself becomes unhealthy.

Separating Interactive Requests From Batch Work

The search and export handlers called the same backend, but one HTTP request did not represent the same amount of work in both cases. An interactive search retrieved a bounded result page while a customer waited. One export could retrieve hundreds of pages and continue long after its submission request had finished.

The team first considered keeping one worker pool and assigning search requests a higher queue priority. That would let a new search move ahead of exports still waiting in the queue. It could do nothing about the six workers already processing exports, though. Those workers would remain occupied until their current jobs yielded or finished.

Baodium gave exports a separate bounded executor. Its workers could read catalog pages and assemble files without occupying threads reserved for interactive requests. A few export workers might be idle when there were no downloads to prepare, but the team accepted that cost to protect customer-facing search capacity.

The new executor needed admission at two points. Before accepting a job, the application checked whether it had room to finish another export under the promised completion policy. Once a job was running, it had to acquire permission for each query it sent to the search cluster. Limiting only the number of export jobs would be insufficient because a single job could issue many backend calls, while limiting only queries would allow an unbounded backlog of accepted jobs.

An export worker also checked for cancellation between pages. If a merchant canceled a download, the worker stopped before issuing its next query. It streamed completed pages to bounded temporary storage instead of collecting the entire catalog in memory. The worker could then release backend capacity while it wrote the page to the file.

Bulkheads and Shared Backend Capacity

Separating executors protected the application’s workers. It did not yet protect the search cluster, which still received queries from both pools.

Chapter 4 introduced a bulkhead, a concurrency limit that prevents one class of work from occupying every available slot. Baodium applied that idea at the point where the search client admitted an outbound query.

Each application process initially had eight backend-call slots. Exports could occupy at most two of them. A query from an export needed an export permit and a shared backend permit, while an interactive search needed only a shared permit.

Suppose both export permits are in use. A third export cannot start another backend query, even when six shared permits happen to be free. Those six are available for interactive searches. When no exports are running, interactive searches may use all eight slots.

The two export permits are a ceiling, rather than capacity reserved for exports. If interactive requests occupy all eight shared slots, an export cannot begin a new query. That may delay its completion, so the export API must not promise a completion deadline that depends on capacity it has not been allocated. Baodium initially favored customer searches and measured export completion separately.

Every export released both permits after retrieving a page, before writing it to its output file. This kept the cluster’s query capacity available while the worker performed local file operations. The team still needed a bounded query deadline so a stalled call could not occupy its permits indefinitely.

Choosing the Per-Process Limit

Why two export permits? The engineers began with estimates and then held the interactive request mix, suggestion traffic, and export sizes constant while varying only the number of simultaneous export queries. Eight export jobs were available throughout each test so a lack of queued work would not conceal the limit.

The interactive search objective was a 95th-percentile latency below 300 milliseconds. One and two permits met it. Four permits increased export throughput only slightly, from 21 to 23 completed jobs per minute, while search p95 rose to 680 milliseconds. The cluster was spending more of its capacity on export queries, leaving interactive requests waiting longer.

The team chose two permits as the starting value. Before production, it repeated the test with large catalogs, uneven traffic, one unavailable application instance, and the planned deployment overlap. Those tests mattered because a setting that passed on one instance could still allow more work than the cluster could sustain across the whole fleet.

Adding Up the Fleet Allocation

The search cluster had sustained 64 concurrent queries under its tested latency target. Indexing and administration tools needed part of that capacity, so the search team allocated 12 slots to indexing and four to administrative queries. That left 48 for the application serving searches, suggestions, and exports.

Four application instances ran normally. A rolling deployment could add a fifth active instance, so the initial design assigned eight backend slots to each process. Five times eight permitted 40 application calls during that surge, leaving eight slots of margin within the application allowance.

Those numbers are ceilings on admitted work under the stated assumptions, not a promise that 64 queries will always complete within the same latency. Query cost changes with search conditions, catalog size, and indexing activity. The cluster still needs admission controls that protect its tested capacity.

The deployment assumption also needs care. As Chapter 6 explained, an old Pod can continue running while its replacement starts. Terminating Pods may still have active connections and queries even when a Deployment’s maxSurge setting is one. If six processes can issue queries during the observed termination overlap, eight permits each would consume all 48 application slots, eliminating the planned margin. Reducing the per-process allocation to seven for that condition would cap those six processes at 42 calls and leave six slots of margin. The team would validate the actual overlap before deciding whether that configuration was sufficient.

A local semaphore cannot enforce the combined fleet limit by itself. Baodium used fixed per-process allocations because traffic among the four normal instances was relatively balanced. A coordinated allocation could redistribute unused permits when instances had uneven demand, but it would introduce a control service and require fencing of expired allocations. For this workload, the engineers preferred a little unused capacity to another dependency in the admission path.

The separate indexing and administration allocations also had to be enforced by their own clients. The search application’s eight permits could not prevent an indexing job from sending 30 queries when its agreed share was twelve.

Accepting Exports as Durable Jobs

After the bulkhead was introduced, interactive searches recovered, but large exports took several minutes. A merchant could no longer assume that a download would finish within one HTTP request, especially if the browser lost its connection midway through the transfer.

Baodium changed the export API to accept a job and return a reference the merchant could use to retrieve its status. The merchant could close the browser and download the file when processing finished.

The job record contained the merchant identity, request parameters, creation time, status, and an idempotency key for repeated submissions. The submission handler authenticated the merchant and checked its export quota before committing the record. A duplicate request for the same accepted export retrieved the earlier job rather than creating another copy. The completed file had a retention period and an access check, and an expired file could be regenerated only through a new authorized job.

Accepting work created an obligation to finish, cancel, or explicitly fail it. That required durable job state and recovery when a worker crashed, just as the payment and fraud workflows in Chapters 3 and 4 required.

The queue also needed a bound. At a measured completion rate of twenty exports per minute, a backlog of one hundred jobs represented about five minutes of processing before additional arrivals, assuming similar job sizes and enough capacity to sustain that rate. A few exceptionally large catalogs could make the waiting time substantially longer.

The team monitored the oldest waiting job, completion throughput, and job sizes. It stopped accepting new exports when the backlog could no longer meet the published completion policy. A merchant whose job had already been accepted could still retrieve its state, while a new submission received a temporary refusal under the API’s quota or capacity contract.

Decision review

Should exports receive more capacity overnight?

Each search application instance has eight backend-call slots, with at most two available for export queries. A merchant reports that an export now takes eleven minutes rather than four. One engineer proposes raising the export limit to six permits at 03:00, when interactive traffic is usually low. Another proposes adding more export workers. A third suggests a separate search replica for exports.

Increase export permits to six during a fixed overnight window.

Keep two permits and add export workers.

Keep the current limit while evaluating a dedicated export replica.

A higher overnight allowance may be acceptable if it is based on measured unused capacity and automatically contracts when interactive demand returns. A fixed clock window cannot account for promotions or customers in other time zones. Adding workers without changing the two backend permits does not raise the limit on simultaneous export queries. A dedicated replica can separate query admission, at the cost of another replica to operate and keep current. Shared indexing, storage, and network capacity may still connect the workloads. Baodium retained the two-permit limit and measured sustained export demand before paying for isolation.

Circuit Breakers When the Cluster Slows Down

The bulkhead helped when exports competed with customer searches. A few weeks later, an index rebuild slowed queries from every caller. Interactive searches, suggestions, and exports all experienced longer responses, even within their admission allocations.

The application was still sending requests to a cluster that was already slow. Each query consumed its deadline and occupied a backend slot while the cluster struggled to finish earlier work.

Chapter 4 introduced the circuit breaker for this situation. It observes recent dependency calls and temporarily refuses new ones when failures or excessive latency indicate that the dependency is unlikely to meet its contract.

A closed breaker permits calls and records their results. An open breaker refuses calls for a configured interval. After that interval, a half-open breaker admits a small number of probes. Successful probes can return it to the closed state, while failure causes it to open again.

The search breaker classified connection failures, timeouts, and calls slower than the tested slow-call threshold as bad observations. An empty result set was a successful search result, so it did not count as a dependency failure. A merchant’s quota rejection also did not count as a cluster failure, since the query had never been admitted to the cluster.

Choosing a Breaker Policy

Baodium’s interactive search client allowed at most 400 milliseconds for one backend attempt, or less when the incoming request’s deadline was closer. Representative successful queries were much faster, so the team selected 250 milliseconds as its slow-call threshold.

attempt:
  maximum_duration_ms: 400

breaker:
  sample_window_seconds: 20
  minimum_completed_calls: 100
  technical_failure_rate: 0.50
  slow_call_duration_ms: 250
  slow_call_rate: 0.30
  open_interval_seconds: 10
  half_open_calls: 3
  half_open_successes_required: 3

These values were part of Baodium’s tested policy, rather than universal recommendations. In a rolling twenty-second observation window containing at least one hundred completed calls, a technical failure rate of at least 50 percent or a slow-call rate of at least 30 percent could open the breaker. The two thresholds captured different problems. A dependency could return valid results that were consistently too slow for checkout or search, just as the fraud provider had done in Chapter 4.

The minimum sample count prevented a handful of failures during a quiet period from opening the breaker. A local breaker implementation evaluates its policy as results arrive, so it does not necessarily wait for a full window before acting once its minimum sample exists. Calls that are still running have contributed no completed result, however. Concurrency admission therefore continues protecting the cluster before the breaker has enough evidence to open.

The ten-second open interval included a small random variation between instances so the whole fleet did not probe at precisely the same moment. Export queries used their own latency thresholds because retrieving an export page could take longer than an ordinary interactive search. Combining those two classes under one slow-call definition would make a healthy export look like an unhealthy search backend.

Libraries such as Resilience4j, Polly, and gobreaker provide circuit breakers. The exact configuration vocabulary differs by library, so the team verified each threshold and state transition in the deployed implementation rather than assuming the illustrative names were portable.

Recovery Probes and Returning Traffic

The half-open probe was a real bounded search query, rather than a health request that established only that the cluster process was reachable. Three successful queries provided evidence that the dependency could answer some calls again. They did not establish that the cluster could handle its full previous workload.

When the breaker closed, the application continued enforcing the same concurrency and rate limits. Export workers resumed in stages, and recovery workers did not release every delayed attempt at once. Otherwise, the accumulated work could reproduce the overload immediately after the first successful probes.

Local breakers introduce another fleet-wide consideration. Five instances may each admit three half-open probes, and restarting an instance may reset its breaker’s local history. A deployment during an outage can therefore produce waves of fresh attempts. The recovery test included that case, and Chapter 6’s liveness probe was kept independent of search-cluster availability to avoid repeated restarts during a shared failure.

Rate Limits and the Caller Who Uses Them

The search team then found another source of unexpected demand. A merchant integration was polling its product listings through eight API keys at a combined 400 requests per second. Its traffic represented roughly one quarter of the cluster’s query load during the measured interval.

The bulkhead limited simultaneous backend queries, but a fast dependency could still complete many calls through the same slots. A rate limit controls how frequently new attempts are admitted, while a concurrency limit controls how many remain in progress. Both are needed when the cluster has limits on query rate and outstanding work.

A Token Bucket

A common rate limiter is a token bucket. Tokens accumulate at a configured rate up to a maximum balance. A request consumes a token when it is admitted. The maximum balance allows a short burst, while the refill rate limits sustained traffic.

Suppose a bucket refills at 100 tokens per second and can contain ten. A caller that has been idle may submit ten attempts immediately, then continue at approximately 100 attempts per second as tokens refill. The burst needs testing because even a short spike can exceed a dependency’s queue or latency allowance.

The monotonic clock avoids disruptions from changes to wall-clock time, and the lock prevents two threads from spending the final token together. This implementation controls one process. If ten application instances each create an identical bucket, the effective fleet allowance may be ten times the intended rate.

A fleet-wide rate limit needs shared enforcement, such as an atomic operation in Redis or an approved gateway rate-limit service. If that coordinator is unavailable, the application needs a defined fallback. For the search API, Baodium used conservative local allowances that fitted within the shared budget during a coordinator failure. Requests beyond those allowances were refused rather than admitted without a limit. That policy was especially important for expensive operations and external providers with contractual limits.

What Identity Defines a Quota?

The merchant’s eight API keys exposed another issue. If each key could send fifty requests per second, the merchant could submit all 400 requests without violating any single-key quota. Creating more keys would raise its effective allowance again.

Limiting requests by IP address would not reliably identify the merchant either. Many customers share corporate or mobile-network addresses, while one integration can send traffic from several addresses.

Baodium resolved each authenticated API key to its merchant and charged all of that merchant’s requests to one tenant allowance. The initial policy admitted twenty search requests per second per merchant, with a burst of forty. A separate fleet-wide allowance protected the cluster when many merchants were active at once.

Both checks were required. The per-merchant limit prevented one merchant from using capacity intended for others, while the fleet-wide limit prevented a large population of individually compliant merchants from exceeding total cluster capacity.

A retry counted against the same merchant allowance as an initial attempt. Merchant identity came from authenticated server-side account records, never an untrusted field supplied by the caller. The application also applied resource authorization before allowing a merchant to search or export another merchant’s data.

The HTTP response reflected the reason for refusal. A tenant exceeding its configured request quota could receive 429 Too Many Requests, with a Retry-After value when the server could estimate a useful retry interval. Temporary cluster-wide overload could instead produce 503 Service Unavailable. Neither response should invite an unbounded client retry loop.1

Retry Budgets and Amplified Load

During the index rebuild, the team found that search clients were retrying calls that timed out. Even one additional attempt per failure could materially increase the load on the cluster.

Suppose 100 original requests arrive each second and 20 percent time out. If each timed-out request is retried once, the cluster receives 100 original attempts and another 20 retries per second. Offered demand rises to 120 attempts per second precisely when the cluster is having difficulty completing its existing work.

Baodium adopted a retry budget limiting additional attempts to five percent of recent original requests. At 100 originals per second, that would allow about five retries per second under sustained conditions, subject to the budget’s interval and burst cap. Some potentially recoverable requests would now receive an unavailable result. The team accepted that tradeoff to avoid adding another fifteen attempts per second to an overloaded cluster.

The budget kept only a limited balance. It could not accumulate unused retry credits all afternoon and spend them in one burst during an outage. Backoff with jitter remained useful for spreading eligible retries over time, but it did not replace the budget because delayed retries still consume capacity when they eventually start.

Each retry also needed to fit the original request deadline and pass the breaker, rate, and concurrency controls. The search client owned the retry policy. The gateway, service mesh, and SDK were configured not to add another layer of automatic retries. Chapter 4 showed how retries nested across several layers can multiply one original request into many more attempts than intended.

A retry waiting through backoff did not occupy a backend-call permit. Export jobs returned to a scheduled state instead of keeping an executor worker asleep while the delay elapsed. A canceled export stopped scheduling additional pages.

Load Shedding and Fallback Responses

The engineers had limited how much work could reach the search cluster. They still needed to decide what customers would receive when a request could not be admitted.

One proposed fallback was to query the primary Catalog database whenever search was unavailable. That sounded convenient because the product records already existed there. It would also direct a surge of expensive search traffic into a database that had not been tested for that query pattern. The fallback could create a second incident.

Baodium chose a narrower option. For popular queries with a suitable cached result, the application could return that result under its documented freshness and access policy. Other queries received a clear temporary unavailable response. An empty result list would have implied that no products matched the query, which the service could not establish while search was unavailable.

Choosing which requests to omit or defer under overload is called load shedding. The useful target is the work consuming the scarce resource. When the cluster is saturated, pausing export queries frees cluster capacity. Disabling an unrelated analytics task that never uses the cluster does not.

Suggestions also used search capacity, and the original two-slot cap covered only exports. The team found that suggestions could consume slots needed by the customer’s submitted search. It therefore replaced the export-only allowance with a shared optional-work allowance. Exports and suggestions together could occupy at most two of the eight backend slots per process.

The team reran the concurrency test with both optional workloads active. Search latency met its target, fewer than one percent of eligible suggestions were omitted at peak, and export throughput fell from about 21 to about 18 jobs per minute. The export completion policy could accommodate that change.

search_cluster_admission:
  shared_backend_slots: 8
  optional_work_slots: 2     # exports and suggestions combined
  interactive_search:
    acquire: shared_backend_slot
    wait: bounded_queue_16_for_at_most_250ms
  search_suggestions:
    acquire: optional_slot_then_shared_slot
    when_refused: omit_module
  merchant_export:
    acquire: optional_slot_then_shared_slot
    when_refused: defer_next_page

This policy limits optional work to two simultaneous queries. It does not reserve the other six for a dedicated search executor, and interactive requests can use every shared slot when they are free. When all eight slots are occupied, interactive requests enter a bounded queue of at most sixteen per process for no more than 250 milliseconds, subject to the incoming request deadline. Those that cannot be admitted return the appropriate temporary-unavailable response.

Within the optional allowance, the application gave suggestions preference over exports when a customer was already waiting. A scheduler could implement that policy through separate bounded queues or admission rules. Whatever mechanism it used, the final semaphore acquisition was atomic. Reading an in-flight gauge and then deciding that a slot was free would permit concurrent callers to oversubscribe the allocation.

These reduced responses apply only where the business contract allows them. A required audit event, payment record, or inventory reservation cannot be silently omitted under the same policy as search suggestions. Deferred work must also have a bounded backlog and recovery capacity.

Priority came from a trusted server-side classification of the operation. If clients could label their own requests as urgent, callers would naturally consume the protected capacity intended for other work.

Implementing Atomic Admission

The concurrency policy depended on acquiring the optional and shared permits without allowing another caller to claim the same capacity. A semaphore provides that atomic local operation.

The following code applies the two limits to one export page. Suggestions use the same optional semaphore, and interactive search uses only the shared semaphore. The deadline and client interfaces are illustrative.

If the optional permit is unavailable, the caller stops before attempting a backend slot. If it acquires the optional permit but finds all backend slots occupied, it returns that permit immediately. The finally blocks release both permits after the local call has finished or its client reports an error.

There is an important limit to the guarantee. A client-side timeout may end the local wait while a search query continues executing in the cluster. Releasing the local permit then allows another query to start, possibly overlapping the abandoned one remotely. A local limit of eight is therefore not proof that the cluster is executing at most eight queries from that process.

The team tested remote cancellation and the search engine’s actual timeout behavior. Elasticsearch, for example, applies search timeouts at particular query phases and may return partial results. A search timeout should not be assumed to stop every remote operation immediately. The backend needs its own admission or cancellation controls, and the capacity plan must allow for work that continues after the caller has disconnected.

The breaker and semaphore rules also interact. If the breaker admits a half-open probe but the local backend slot is unavailable, that is a local admission refusal, not evidence that the cluster failed. The implementation returns the probe allowance without counting a failed dependency call.

The team tested these partial-acquisition paths for permit leaks and misclassified failures. A small bug in admission cleanup can gradually reduce available concurrency even when the search backend is healthy.

State-Changing Operations Need a Different Refusal Contract

A rejected search has not changed a business record. Payment, inventory, and refund operations require more care because a remote action may have completed before a timeout reached the caller.

Before dispatch, an admission refusal means the new attempt did not start. After dispatch, a timeout may leave the remote outcome uncertain. The application must inspect the durable operation and use its provider’s reconciliation contract before inviting another attempt.

Chapter 3 established that rule for payments. Chapter 4 carried it into deferred fraud assessment. The same distinction applies to rate limits and circuit breakers in this chapter.

A payment provider’s breaker may refuse new authorizations while existing ones remain unresolved. Status queries, provider reconciliation, and corrective operations may need separate reserved capacity so the system can finish investigating earlier requests even while new purchases are being refused.

An application should therefore measure admission refusals alongside business outcomes. A faster response time can be misleading when the improvement comes from rejecting nearly every request before work begins.

Testing Overload and Recovery Together

By the time Baodium returned to production testing, search had separate execution pools, per-workload admission, a circuit breaker, merchant quotas, and a retry budget. The engineers tested these controls together because their interactions mattered most when capacity was scarce.

The test used an open-loop load generator that maintained the expected interactive arrival rate while exports processed realistic catalogs. The engineers increased export demand until the optional allowance was full, then checked that interactive p95 remained under its objective and that every refused job or query had the expected outcome.

Next, the test delayed cluster responses and held some calls open. This exercised the period before the breaker had enough completed failures to open. The engineers measured actual backend query concurrency as well as local permits, since cancellation could cause those numbers to diverge.

Finally, the cluster recovered while export jobs, suggestions, and retry candidates were waiting. The application had to resume them within the same capacity budget, without creating another surge. The test continued until the accepted backlog had either completed or reached its documented terminal outcome.

The team repeated the cases with one application instance unavailable and during a rolling deployment. Those conditions changed the number of local limiters that could send work to the shared cluster.

The report included accepted, completed, rejected, timed-out, and pending requests, along with queue age, cluster latency, and business completion rates. Every admission refusal recorded its policy version and reason: merchant quota, optional-work limit, shared backend capacity, or open breaker. That made an overload investigation much faster than a dashboard showing only a generic error count.

Field note

Amazon S3, February 2017

On February 28, 2017, an authorized engineer was investigating slow processing in Amazon S3’s billing system in the US-EAST-1 region. A command intended to remove a small number of servers received an incorrect input and removed far more capacity than intended.

The affected servers supported S3’s index and placement subsystems, which were required for core object-storage operations. Both subsystems needed recovery, and their full restarts took substantially longer than the team had previously experienced at smaller scale.

AWS subsequently changed the operational tool so capacity could be removed more slowly and an action could not take a subsystem below its minimum required capacity. Those controls limited how much damage one permitted maintenance action could cause.

The incident also exposed a recovery assumption. A procedure that works quickly at a small scale may take much longer after the system has grown. Baodium’s load-shedding and recovery tests follow the same principle: the capacity checks and restart procedures must be tested against the scale at which they will actually be used.

Source: AWS’s published S3 service-disruption summary.

Applying the Controls to a Third-Party API

The search cluster belonged to Baodium. Similar capacity limits apply when the dependency is operated by another company and its allowance is part of a service contract.

Consider a SaaS product that sends customer documents to an analysis API. The provider permits 1,000 requests per second for the organization. One tenant starts an import generating 800 requests per second, while all other tenants together generate another 500. Sending all 1,300 exceeds the provider’s allowance before retries are considered.

The application needs a fleet-wide rate limit below or equal to the contractual ceiling and a per-tenant quota that prevents one customer from consuming the entire allocation. The total limit must also account for critical operations requiring capacity when batch imports are active.

A separate concurrency limit is necessary because provider latency can increase without changing the permitted request rate. If a provider call takes six times longer at the same arrival rate, its average number of outstanding requests increases by roughly a factor of six while the system remains stable, as the relationship in Chapter 2 predicts. The concurrency limit may therefore begin refusing work long before the rate limit is reached.

The team also has to decide what happens when the global rate-limit coordinator fails. For an expensive paid API, a conservative local allowance or temporary refusal may be preferable to exceeding the contract. A tenant quota rejection must not count as provider failure in the circuit breaker, and retries consume the original tenant’s quota.

For deferred document analysis, the product needs a bounded queue, expiration policy, and a completion rate that can reduce the backlog while new requests continue arriving. The status API must remain available even when new document analyses cannot be admitted.

Design Exercise: Admission Control for a Reporting API

Imagine a SaaS analytics product whose customers retrieve dashboard summaries through an API. Most queries finish in less than 100 milliseconds, but a full data export may run for several minutes against the same database. Last month, one customer’s nightly export script slowed every interactive dashboard for nearly an hour.

How should the next version treat those two workloads? We can begin by tracing the resources they share. Dashboard queries need low latency and bounded waits. Exports need durable job identity, a completion policy, and limits on the database connections and query time they consume.

The first design gives exports a separate worker pool and a small share of backend capacity. A dashboard request acquires interactive capacity under its deadline. An export submission first passes a tenant job quota and backlog-admission check, then returns a job reference. Running export workers acquire backend capacity for each query rather than keeping a database connection assigned while they assemble a file.

The API applies a per-tenant quota and a global database allowance. A customer who exceeds its quota receives a clear refusal with a useful retry policy, while a repeated request for an accepted export retrieves the existing job. Retries count against the tenant’s allowance, and workers stop dispatching after cancellation or expiry.

A read replica is another option for long export queries. It can separate some reporting work from the primary, although a PostgreSQL standby still needs its own capacity plan. Long queries can conflict with WAL replay and may be canceled or contribute to replay delay under the selected configuration. The product would have to define how incomplete or stale exports are handled.

The recovery test is as important as the overload test. Suppose the database slows for an hour and two hundred exports are waiting when it recovers. Starting every job together would bring back the same problem. The revised system admits a measured number of export queries, confirms that dashboard latency meets its objective, and continues until the accepted backlog has been resolved.

The result is a design with explicit tradeoffs. A merchant may wait longer for a report, and some new exports may be refused during an incident. Those outcomes are visible to the customer and can be checked against the product’s promises. Interactive dashboards have capacity protected from batch work, and the database is not asked to complete more operations than its tested allocation permits.

Summary

Baodium’s search application had not changed when its latency began increasing. The new demand came from merchant exports that shared workers and backend query capacity with customer searches. Separating the workers protected interactive execution. Limiting each export page’s backend calls reduced the demand reaching the cluster.

The later index rebuild required another response. A circuit breaker stopped sending calls that were unlikely to finish within their budgets. Merchant rate limits prevented one integration from consuming a shared allowance, and a retry budget kept timeouts from generating more traffic against an already slow dependency.

All of those controls needed a customer-facing outcome. Baodium could omit suggestions, defer exports, or return a temporary-unavailable search response under the appropriate contract. Payment and inventory operations still required durable identity and reconciliation if their remote outcomes became uncertain.

The final test was recovery. Releasing deferred jobs and retries without admission controls could repeat the original overload just as the cluster became healthy again. The release procedure therefore measured both the ability to contain demand and the time needed to clear accepted work.

Chapter 10 examines the next source of unexpected demand: an application deployment that changes how much capacity each request uses. We will use these measurements and admission policies to decide how much of a new version to expose and when a rollout should be stopped.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & Interactive searches, suggestions, and exports can share the cluster within tested concurrency and rate limits. Exports use a separate worker pool.
Condition that tests it & Export demand rises, queries slow down, retries increase, or deferred jobs resume after an outage or deployment.
Constraint or invariant & Each process permits eight backend calls, including at most two optional calls. Fleet budgets include other cluster users, overlapping instances, and remote work continuing after local timeouts. Job admission is bounded.
Evidence and uncertainty & Two export permits produced search p95 of 210 ms and 21 exports/min. Four raised search p95 to 680 ms for only 23 exports/min. The cluster’s tested concurrent capacity was 64, with 16 allocated to background callers.

Still unknown: remote cancellation effectiveness, unusually expensive queries, and actual deployment overlap.
Signal and evaluation window & Measure search p95, backend concurrency, refusals by policy, retry rate, breaker decisions, and oldest export-job age throughout overload and recovery.
Control and decision & Refuse or defer excess work before dispatch. Protect searches from optional queries, cap retries, and resume deferred traffic under tested limits.
Owner and review trigger & Search owns backend admission. The merchant team owns export commitments. Platform validates fleet and recovery capacity. Review after overload, failed recovery tests, or capacity changes.

  1. RFC 6585 defines 429 for rate limiting. RFC 9110 defines 503 for temporary service unavailability and describes Retry-After.↩︎
